meta.blurb: Showman P. T. Barnum made a fortune, lost nearly all of it when a clock company failed, and began again. At seventy he wrote down his golden rules: choose the right work, avoid debt, advertise and keep your good name.
meta.bible: Phineas Taylor Barnum: American showman, born in Bethel, Connecticut, in 1810, died in Bridgeport in 1891; called Barnum in the book. The Art of Money Getting, or Golden Rules for Making Money: his book of 1880, based on lectures he gave for years. Bethel: his birthplace in Connecticut. Bridgeport: the Connecticut town where he lived. Connecticut. New York. American Museum: the museum he bought in 1841. Tom Thumb: stage name of Charles Stratton, a very small boy from Connecticut whom Barnum made famous. Jenny Lind: Swedish singer who toured America in 1850 for Barnum, who had never heard her sing. Iranistan: his grand house, lost in the 1850s. Jerome Clock Company: a Connecticut clock company whose notes Barnum signed; it failed in the mid-1850s and he went bankrupt. James Bailey: his circus partner. Jumbo: a huge elephant Barnum bought from the London Zoo in 1882. Ecclesiastes: the Bible book that says whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might. Greatest Show on Earth: the circus slogan. Fixed facts: American Museum bought 1841; circus opened 1871; Barnum was mayor of Bridgeport and served in the Connecticut legislature. The saying that a sucker is born every minute is often linked to his name, but there is no good evidence he said it. Voice and tone: practical, concrete and kind, one rule at a time, with Barnum's own life as the example; his weak points are named fairly.

B1B2: In 1880 the famous showman Barnum, who was then about seventy, published a book called The Art of Money Getting. It gathered the golden rules for making money that he had been teaching in lectures for years.
Barnum was born in Bethel, Connecticut, in 1810, and he started work in a village shop while he was still a boy. There he learned how people buy and sell, and he never lost his love of trade.
In 1841 Barnum bought a museum in New York and filled it with animals, wonders and shows. Tickets were not expensive, so crowds came, and families could spend a whole day there.
Barnum made stars of two very different people in the 1840s and 1850s. One was Charles Stratton, a small boy known as Tom Thumb, and the other was the Swedish singer Jenny Lind.
In the mid-1850s Barnum lost most of his money. He had guaranteed the debts of a clock company, and when it failed, he was left owing a huge sum.
Barnum paid back what he owed by lecturing and by working hard again. In 1871 he started a travelling circus, and later he joined James Bailey to make a famous show.
Barnum wrote that money is like fire, a very good servant but a terrible master. He believed that anyone can learn to earn it, if they follow some simple rules.
Barnum's first rule is not to mistake your vocation, which means the kind of work you do. Some people are made for trade, some for farming and some for science, and each does best in the right place.
Barnum noticed that people often fail because they chose the wrong work, and not because they are lazy. He advised readers to find where their natural talents lie and to put all their effort there.
Barnum's second rule is to choose the right place for your business. A good shop in the wrong place may fail, while a plain one in the right place may do very well.
Barnum's third rule is to keep out of debt from the very beginning. A person who owes money cannot rest easily, he said, because the bills grow while he waits.
A man who owes nothing, Barnum said, can follow his own judgment and walk away from a bad bargain. A man who is deep in debt must do whatever his creditors want.
Barnum's next rule is a very simple one, which is to persevere. Many people begin well but quit when trouble comes, and he said that those who keep going are the ones who win.
Barnum knew from his own life that losing money is not the end of everything. After his bankruptcy he worked his way back, and he showed that a determined person can begin again.
Barnum's fifth rule is to do whatever you do with all your might. He quoted an old saying from the Bible and believed that half-hearted work seldom succeeds.
Barnum had little patience with people who waited for luck to find them. In his view, the busiest people are usually the ones whom luck seems to visit.
Barnum's next rule is to depend on yourself and not to take too many partners. Those who lean on others, he said, often fall when the others fail.

Barnum's next rule is to use the best tools, and by tools he meant good workers as well as good machines. He believed a clever employee is worth a good salary, because a poor one costs a business more in the end.
Barnum said that an owner should look for the best helpers and then pay them fairly. Workers who are paid well and treated kindly are likely to stay and to serve the business well.
Barnum's rule here is a warning against getting above your own business. Some people, once they succeed, spend too much on show and forget the work that made them rich.
Barnum urged every young person to learn something useful, such as a trade or a craft. A skill can be a safe base when fortunes change, because nobody can take it from you.
Barnum's next rule is to let hope predominate, which means being hopeful and cheerful. He believed that a hopeful person works better and recovers more quickly than someone who expects the worst.
Barnum also warned against being too visionary, or full of grand and unlikely dreams. A person who spends all day dreaming of a huge fortune may forget to do the careful work that builds a small one.
Barnum's rule is not to scatter your powers over too many different things. He advised readers to choose one kind of business and to stay with it faithfully until they succeed.
Barnum's rule here is to be systematic, which means to keep your affairs in good order. A person who keeps neat accounts and plans each day sees mistakes early and does more in less time.

Barnum said that the owner of a business must watch even the smallest details of it. He should choose his assistants well, and then check their work, because in the end the owner answers for everything.
Barnum strongly advised every person in business to read the newspapers. A person who knows what is happening in the world sees new chances and dangers earlier than one who does not.
Barnum also warned against what he called outside operations. A man who is doing well in his own trade, he said, should not risk his money in schemes that he does not understand.
Barnum warned readers never to endorse another person's debts without security. If that person fails to pay, the one who signed must pay instead, and many good businesses have been ruined this way.
Barnum knew about this danger from his own painful experience in the 1850s. He had signed notes for a clock company, and when it failed he lost a very large part of what he owned.
Barnum, the great showman, said that every business should advertise. A shop may be excellent, but people will not come if they have never heard of it.
Barnum used every kind of advertising he could find, from newspaper notices to posters and handbills. He believed that a good advertisement must catch the eye and give people a reason to come.
Advertising is only the first step, because it can bring a person to the door only once. Good goods and good manners are what make that person come again.
Barnum's rule for dealing with customers is to be polite and kind to all of them. A friendly word and a patient answer cost nothing, he said, yet they bring buyers back again and again.
Barnum said that a shop is known by its people. An owner should choose helpers who are patient and cheerful, because customers remember how they were treated.
Barnum's rule on charity is that people who can afford it should give to those in need. He believed that giving brings joy, and that a person who gives with a warm heart is never really poorer.
Barnum added that charity must be given with good sense. He advised people to help those who truly need it, and to give according to their means rather than what they cannot afford.
Another of Barnum's rules is short and plain, which is not to blab. A person who talks too much about his plans and his money may let others use his ideas or take advantage of him.
Barnum's closing rule is to preserve your integrity, which means to be honest in everything. A good name is the best thing a person can own, he said, and once it is lost it is very hard to win back.
Barnum saw honesty as a matter of good business as well as of right and wrong. People return to a shop that deals fairly, and they tell others to come as well.

Barnum's critics often called him a humbug, and he certainly loved to surprise and amaze the public. The saying that a sucker is born every minute is often linked to his name, but there is no good evidence that he said it.

Some of Barnum's advice sounds old-fashioned now, for example his praise of the daily newspaper. Yet most of his central ideas, such as avoiding debt and treating customers well, still make good sense.
Taken together, Barnum's rules form a kind of path from start to finish. First you choose the right work, then you work hard and keep order, and last you treat others honestly.
A reader does not need to use all the rules at once. It is easier to choose one, such as keeping neat accounts or avoiding new debts, and to practise it until it becomes a habit.
Barnum served in the Connecticut legislature, became mayor of Bridgeport and bought the huge elephant Jumbo in 1882. He died in 1891 at the age of eighty, still famous across the world.
In Barnum's view, money is only valuable for what it lets a person do. It brings independence and comfort, and it gives a way of helping other people.
Barnum did not hide his failures in his writing. He told of his mistakes openly, because he believed that a person who learns from them can turn them into something useful.
If Barnum's long list had to be cut to five ideas, they might be these. Find the right work, work with all your might, keep out of debt, serve people kindly and stay honest.
Barnum never promised that anyone could get rich overnight. He offered a long and steady road instead, and he said that those who stay on it with patience will arrive in the end.

The art of money getting, in Barnum's book, comes down to right work, steady habits and honest dealing. A person who follows these rules, and who uses the money well, can be wealthy in the best sense of the word.
C1C2: In 1880, when he was nearly seventy years old, the great American showman Phineas Barnum put his advice about money into a short book with a long title, The Art of Money Getting, or Golden Rules for Making Money. He had given lectures on the subject for years and had made, lost and made again a very large fortune, so he spoke from experience rather than from theory. The rules he gave are simple and practical, and many of them sound as sensible today as they did then.

Phineas Taylor Barnum was born in 1810 in the small town of Bethel in Connecticut, and as a boy he worked in a village shop where he learned how people bargain and how they spend. Over the following years he tried a number of trades, from storekeeping to publishing a small weekly newspaper, before he found the one that made him famous. Everything he later wrote about business grew out of these early lessons and out of the mistakes he made along the way.

In 1841 Barnum bought the American Museum in New York, a dusty collection that was failing, and he turned it into the most talked-about place in the city. He filled it with curiosities, living animals, lectures and shows, and he advertised it so cleverly that families came in crowds to see what the fuss was about. The museum made him famous, and it also taught him the lessons about customers, advertising and hard work that fill his book.

Barnum's great talent for finding people whom the public wanted to see was what first made him rich. He took a small boy from Connecticut, Charles Stratton, and made him famous as General Tom Thumb, and in 1850 he brought the Swedish singer Jenny Lind to tour America, even though he had never heard her sing. Her concerts drew large crowds and a great deal of money, and they showed how much a good name and a good advertisement could do.

Barnum's own life was proof that even a very large fortune can vanish almost overnight, however carefully it was built. In the mid-1850s he had lent his name to a clock company in Connecticut, guaranteeing its debts, and when the company failed he was left owing an enormous sum and was forced into bankruptcy. His grand house, Iranistan, was lost, and the hard lesson shaped several of the rules in his book.

Barnum met his troubles by lecturing, writing and building new businesses until his debts were paid and his name was strong again. In 1871, when most men think of retirement, he opened a huge travelling circus, and a few years later he joined forces with James Bailey to create the show that became famous as the Greatest Show on Earth. He was still working when he wrote his book of rules, which is perhaps the best evidence that he believed them.

Barnum begins from a plain belief, which is that anyone willing to learn and to work can follow the road to wealth, whatever the starting point. Money, he wrote, is in some respects like fire, for it is an excellent servant but a terrible master, and he wanted his readers to command it rather than be commanded by it. His twenty or so rules, taken one at a time, are meant to show how.

The first rule in Barnum's book warns against mistaking one's vocation, since a person put into the wrong kind of work is like a good tool used for the wrong job. A man who would make an excellent farmer may be a poor shopkeeper, and a born salesman may be miserable behind a plough, and neither will prosper until he finds the work that suits him. Barnum counselled the young to think carefully about their natural gifts before they spent years on any trade.

Barnum had watched many failures, and he thought that a large share of them came not from laziness or bad luck but from a simple mismatch between a person and a job. Someone with a gift for dealing with people may be wasted at a desk, and someone with a gift for figures may be wasted at a market stall. The remedy, he said, is to study oneself honestly and then to pick the work in which one's strengths can be used to the full.

Barnum's second rule concerns place, for he knew that a shop can be well stocked, honestly run and still go bankrupt if it stands where no customers pass. A trader, he said, must go where the people are, whether that means a busy street, a growing town or a new settlement that needs what he sells. The same advice applies today to the choice of a city, a neighbourhood or a website.

Debt, Barnum warned, is one of the heaviest burdens a young person can carry, for it turns a man into a servant of those to whom he owes money and takes away his peace of mind. Those who begin by borrowing for comforts they cannot afford often find that interest and anxiety grow faster than their earnings. His advice was to live within one's means, to pay as one goes, and to borrow only with the greatest care.

Freedom, in Barnum's eyes, was the great reward of keeping out of debt, and he valued it above many comforts. The person who owes nothing may use his own judgment, refuse a bad bargain and wait patiently for a good opportunity, whereas a person in debt must please his creditors and cannot afford to wait. Independence of this kind, Barnum suggested, is the foundation on which every other business rule rests.

Barnum's fourth rule is perseverance, and he treated it almost as a law of nature, since few good things come to those who quit at the first obstacle. When a person has chosen the right work and the right place, he argued, he should stay with them through disappointment, for those who keep trying are the ones who finally succeed. Many failures, in his view, were people who stopped just before the point at which their work would have paid.

Barnum could speak about perseverance with some authority, because his own bankruptcy had left him owing a fortune at an age when many men hope to rest. He did not sit in despair, but instead lectured, wrote, planned and worked until he had built a new fortune, and his example suggests that the same road lies open to anyone who is determined enough. The lesson, then, is not that failure never comes, but that it need not be final.

Barnum's fifth rule is taken from an old saying in the Book of Ecclesiastes, that whatever your hand finds to do, you should do it with all your might. He insisted that half-hearted effort rarely produces more than half-hearted results, and that the people who rise are usually the ones who put their whole mind and energy into each task. A person who works only when he feels like it, he suggested, will never keep up with one who works every day.

To Barnum, luck was a poor excuse for those who had not tried, and he noticed that the busiest people always seemed to be the ones whom fortune favoured. By working with all his might, a man increases the number of chances he meets and the skill with which he can use them. In this sense, effort and good fortune are partners rather than rivals, and the first is far more often within our control.

Barnum advised his readers to depend upon themselves, and not to take too many partners into a business. A man who leans on other people's money, other people's skill and other people's decisions, he said, is likely to fall when they fail him, and too many voices in a partnership can make sound decisions impossible. A person who wants to succeed should learn to rely first of all on his own energy and judgment.

The next rule is to use the best tools, and Barnum was careful to explain that the finest tools are not machines but people. He thought it wise to find skilful, honest and sober helpers and to pay them well, because a first-class employee earns far more than he costs, whereas a cheap and careless one can ruin a business. An employer, he implied, should be judged by the quality of those who work for him.

Having found good people, Barnum argued, an employer should reward them fairly, for a worker who feels that he is properly paid is likely to give honest and willing service. A business that is always changing its staff to save a few dollars, he warned, pays the cost in mistakes and lost customers. It is better to keep a skilled assistant on a generous wage than to hire a stranger on a poor one.

Barnum had seen successful people grow proud, begin to spend on fine houses and grand appearances, and gradually lose interest in the plain work that had made them prosperous. Such a person, he warned, is likely to find his affairs sinking while his vanity rises. To keep what one has won, he said, one must go on watching the business closely, however comfortable one has become.

Another of Barnum's rules is that every person should learn something useful, a trade or a craft or a profession on which to rely. Fortunes rise and fall, as he knew well, but a skill that people will pay for cannot be seized or lost in a bad year. Even the rich, he thought, should know how to do something worthwhile with their hands or their minds.

Barnum wished his readers to let hope predominate, by which he meant that a person should face the world with a cheerful and confident spirit. Gloomy people, he thought, see difficulties everywhere and often give up before they have begun, whereas hopeful people see openings and have the energy to use them. Hope, in this sense, is not a dream but a working habit of the mind.

Hope, Barnum added, must be balanced by good sense, for the visionary man who chases enormous schemes often neglects the ordinary tasks that would bring him a steady income. He had little respect for those who expected to be rich overnight by some wonderful invention or lucky speculation. A sound plan, a careful count of costs and a willingness to start small were, to him, better guides than a splendid dream.

A man who tries to do five things at once, Barnum said, will usually do none of them well, and his rule was therefore to engage in one kind of business and stick to it faithfully. Success comes from concentrating one's time, money and attention on a single purpose until it is firmly established. Only when experience shows that the chosen path is hopeless, he thought, should a person consider leaving it.

Barnum was a great believer in system, by which he meant order in one's accounts, one's time and one's dealings with others. A business run without method, he said, loses money without anyone noticing, and mistakes are found too late. He recommended that every person should have a place and a plan for everything, and should know at all times exactly where he stands.

System, Barnum implied, also means giving close attention to the smallest details, because large failures so often begin as small ones that nobody examined. An employer should pick his assistants with care, explain exactly what he wants and then look over what they have done, since it is his name and his money that are at risk. The habit of regular inspection costs little time and may save a great deal of trouble.

Barnum was himself a man of the press, and he urged every reader to take a good newspaper and read it regularly. A person who follows the news, he argued, knows what the world is doing, what it needs and what it is beginning to fear, and he is therefore better placed to see opportunities and to avoid hazards. To neglect the paper, in his view, was to do business with one's eyes half closed.

One of Barnum's strongest warnings was against outside operations, meaning the habit of putting money into mines, land schemes or speculations that have nothing to do with one's own business. A man who knows his trade thoroughly and does well in it, he argued, often loses what he has earned by risking it where he knows nothing. His advice was to give one's money the same close attention as one's work, and to be wary of any promise of quick and easy gains.

To endorse a note is to promise to pay another person's debt if he cannot, and Barnum warned that no one should do it without proper security. Many an honest and prosperous man had been dragged down, he said, by the failure of a friend whose paper he had signed in a moment of kindness. Kindness is no excuse, he insisted, for staking one's whole fortune on another person's good luck.

Barnum was not preaching from a distance, for he had learned this lesson in the hardest possible way when the clock company whose notes he had signed collapsed. He was left to answer for sums far larger than he had ever imagined, and the loss of his fortune and his house followed. The story gave special weight to the rule, and it showed that even a clever and successful man may be caught by a moment of misplaced trust.

As a showman, Barnum was a master of publicity, and he insisted that every business owner should advertise, since no shop can serve customers who do not know it exists. The finest goods, honestly priced, will still lie unsold on the shelves if nobody is told about them. A man who hides his light under a bushel, he implied, has only himself to blame when others pass by.

Barnum himself used every form of publicity that his age offered, including newspaper notices, posters, handbills and signs painted on walls, and he believed in repeating a message until the public could not fail to notice it. A good advertisement, in his view, is one that attracts attention, tells people something interesting and gives them a reason to visit the shop. He regarded the cost of advertising not as an expense to be avoided but as an investment that returns more than it takes.

Advertising, as Barnum's rules taken together suggest, is only the beginning of the work, for it can bring a customer to the door but cannot make him return. What brings him back is the quality of the goods, the fairness of the price and the courtesy with which he is treated, which are the subjects of the rules that follow. A business built on advertisement alone is therefore like a fine sign over an empty shop.

Barnum insisted that every person who deals with the public should be polite and kind to everyone who comes to the shop, whether the customer is rich or poor, and whether he buys or merely looks. A pleasant word and a patient answer cost nothing, he reasoned, and they bring in a steady stream of loyal customers who tell their friends. A single rude clerk, on the other hand, can undo the work of all the advertising in the world.

A shop, Barnum observed, is judged by those who stand behind its counter, and the owner is wise who chooses assistants of good manners and good temper. Customers forget a small saving in price much more readily than they forget a sharp word, and they will gladly walk past a cheaper shop to reach one where they are welcomed. Kindness to the customer is therefore not a luxury, but a plain business advantage.

Barnum asked the successful to be charitable, and he regarded giving to those in real need as a duty and a pleasure rather than a loss. The man who hoards everything and shares nothing, he said, is poor in spirit however large his bank account may be. Money that is given with a warm heart and a clear head does good in the world and leaves the giver richer in the respect of others.

Charity, however, needs good sense as well as a warm heart, and Barnum cautioned his readers to give where help is truly needed and likely to be well used. A person should give according to his means, neither refusing everyone out of meanness nor giving so much that his own family suffers. Wise generosity, he implied, is part of a well-ordered life, just like saving and working.

Barnum's rule against blabbing recommends keeping one's own counsel, for the person who tells everyone about his plans, his profits and his troubles gives his rivals a free lesson. A clever idea shared too early may be copied by someone with more money, and a business trouble spoken of too freely may frighten away the very friends who could help. Say little about what you intend to do, he advised, and let the results of your work speak for you when the time comes.

The final rule in Barnum's list is to preserve one's integrity, for he held that character is the most valuable property a person can possess. A man with a reputation for honest dealing, he argued, has credit, customers and friends, while one who has been caught in dishonesty will find the doors of trade closing against him. No gain, however large, could be worth the price of losing one's good name.

Honesty, Barnum thought, is not merely a moral duty but also the soundest business policy, since customers who have been treated fairly return again and bring their neighbours with them. Trust, once earned, becomes a kind of capital that cannot be seen on any balance sheet but that supports every sale. He therefore ended his rules where a wise teacher should, with the quality that gives all the others their value.

Barnum's reputation was always mixed, for his enemies called him a humbug and he rather enjoyed playing the part of a man who could surprise and amaze the public. The famous remark that a sucker is born every minute is often linked to his name, though historians have found no good evidence that he said it. Some of his early exhibits are now seen as unkind to the people on show, so it is fair to read his rules as a skilful businessman's advice and not as a model for his whole life.

Several of Barnum's examples belong to the world of the horse and the printing press, and his remarks on newspapers and handbills would need to be rewritten for the age of the internet. Yet the principles underneath them, such as avoiding debt, working hard, treating customers kindly and never staking more than one can afford, have changed very little. That is probably why a book of 1880 can still be read with profit by anyone who earns or spends money.

Read together, Barnum's rules fall into a natural order, beginning with the choice of work and place, moving through the habits of energy, system and prudence, and ending with courtesy, generosity and honesty toward others. Each rule supports the others, for a person who keeps out of debt can afford to be honest, and a person who is honest earns the trust that brings customers. They are less a list of tricks than a description of a steady, practical character.

A reader does not need to adopt every rule at once, and the sensible way to use Barnum's advice is to take one at a time. Begin, perhaps, with the habit that seems most lacking, whether it is keeping neat accounts, staying out of debt, learning a useful skill or speaking more kindly to customers, and practise it until it becomes second nature. Small habits, steadily kept over many months and years, are in the end the real art of money getting.

In his later years Barnum served in the Connecticut legislature, became mayor of Bridgeport, and bought Jumbo, the huge elephant from the London Zoo, whom he showed to crowds across America. He kept working almost to the end, and he died in 1891 at the age of eighty, having seen his name become a byword for showmanship all over the world. His book of rules has been reprinted many times, and it is still read for the good sense that runs through it.

Throughout his book Barnum treats money as a tool rather than as an end in itself, valuable because it can purchase independence, comfort for one's family and the means to help others. The person who loves it for its own sake, he suggested, becomes its slave, whereas one who uses it well finds that it serves a larger purpose. This is the meaning of his image of fire, which warms the house when it is controlled and burns it down when it is not.

A striking feature of Barnum's writing is that he does not pretend to have been wiser than he was, and he is willing to tell of his own failures as well as his triumphs. A mistake honestly faced, he seems to say, becomes a teacher, whereas a mistake hidden is simply repeated. His readers, trusting a man who had lost a fortune and won another, were more ready to take his advice.

If one had to reduce Barnum's long list to five ideas, they might be to find suitable work, give it full energy, keep debts under control, serve others with courtesy and guard one's good name. Everything else in the book is an elaboration or an example of one of these themes. A reader who followed even this short list faithfully would, by Barnum's reckoning, be well on the road to wealth.

Barnum never claimed that wealth could be had overnight, and indeed he had harsh words for those who looked for easy fortunes and quick gains. What he offered instead was a long, steady road made of small choices, such as the choice to work, to save, to be fair and to persevere, each of which seems minor but adds up over years. It is a humbler promise than that of a get-rich scheme, but it is also a far more reliable one.

The art of money getting, as Barnum taught it, is no secret or trick but a matter of choosing the right work, working with all one's might, keeping out of debt, treating others kindly and holding fast to one's honesty. Those who follow these rules patiently may well become wealthy, and those who also give generously and keep their good name will find their wealth worth having. It was a plain lesson from a man whose life had been anything but plain, and it still deserves to be heard.
